newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek labour unions join farmers' protest.
newsitem.headline: Greek labour unions join farmers' protest.

text.p: Greek workers joined demonstrating farmers on Monday, beginning a week of strikes and marches to protest against the socialist government's tough 1997 budget.
Teachers and seamen opened the week of strikes by Greece's biggest labour confederations, representing civil servants, workers, doctors, bank employees and even diplomats.
The strikes, all aimed at securing better pay, precede the vote in parliament on the budget next Saturday at midnight after a five-day debate.

The farmers, who have blocked national roads for 19 days, have threatened to invade Athens on Wednesday while Greece's biggest labour confederation, GSEE, which has about a million members, has invited unions to a protest march for Tuesday.
Boat schedules were cancelled on Monday, the first day of a two-day seamen's strike and schools sent students away after the teachers also walked out for two days.
Public servants go on a one-day strike on Tuesday, when customs officials begin a three-day walkout, while doctors have been on a seven-day strike since last Wednesday.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who returned on Sunday from a European Union summit in Dublin, has refused all demands, saying they would prevent Greece from reaching its EU convergence targets.
The budget, aimed at helping Greece qualify to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 2001, cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes new taxes.
It is designed to bring the state about $4 billion from the extra taxes and spending cuts next year. The socialists have described the budget as the harshest in 15 years.

In his first crisis since winning elections in September, Simitis has drawn criticism for doing nothing but wait for the farmers to tire of their crippling blockade, which has cost the economy millions of dollars.
"We can and must start a national dialogue on farmers' problems," government spokesman Yannis Nikolaou said. "But this cannot happen under the pressure of blocked national roads."

Pressing for cheaper fuel and state subsidies for products, the farmers have kept up five major blockades with thousands of tractors along the main north-south highway and threaten to continue their action over the Christmas holidays.
"The government holds the key to this dead end," farmers' representative Yannis Patakis told reporters. "The prime minister is pouring oil on the fire with his intransigence."
Smaller blockades exist around the country although a number have been removed on backroads in recent days.

"He (Simiti) feels that if he gives in now, then every time a group wants something they will block the roads," a senior government official told Reuters. "He refuses to use the police, so his only choice is to wait."
But reaction is growing even within his government.
"We should not base our national policy on the threat: Maastricht (EMU) or catastrophe," Education Minister Gerassimos Arsenis told an Athens newspaper. "People can't be motivated by such dilemmas."

Simitis held the third cabinet meeting in two weeks on Monday to discuss the farmers' revolt. Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos, the government's number two, urged Simitis to meet the farmers and discuss their problems.
Tsohatzopoulos is among those in the socialist party who fear the political cost of alienating farmers, who have been the party's backbone for many years.
The streets of Athens echo daily to the chants of unhappy workers, pensioners, students and customs employees protesting against the tight incomes policy.
Even diplomats, the most loyal of civil servants, have joined the strikes to protest against a new tax on an allowance given to diplomats abroad to cover living and travelling costs.
